questions.stemHtml: Gland around pigmented area is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Modified sebaceous gland

 

The arrow is pointing towards the montgomery tubercles present in areola and not the whole breast.

 

Montgomery tubercles are modified sebaceous glands that serve a protective function.

 

Key Features:

 

  1. Montgomery’s Tubercles:
    • Found in the areolar region surrounding the nipple.
    • Secrete a lipid-rich substance to keep the nipple and areola lubricated and prevent cracking during breastfeeding.
    • This secretion also has antimicrobial properties to protect the area.
  2. Breast Gland Types:
    • The breast as a whole is a modified sweat gland, but Montgomery’s tubercles are distinct as they are sebaceous glands.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Modified sweat gland: The entire breast gland is a modified sweat gland, but Montgomery’s tubercles specifically are sebaceous glands.

 

Option C. Holocrine gland: While sebaceous glands function in a holocrine manner, this option is too broad and does not specifically refer to Montgomery's tubercles.

 

Option D. Merocrine gland: Refers to glands like eccrine sweat glands, unrelated to Montgomery’s tubercles.

 

Educational objective:

 

Montgomery’s tubercles are modified sebaceous glands in the areola that provide lubrication and protection, especially during breastfeeding. The correct answer is B. Modified sebaceous gland.

options.label: A
options.text: Fibrosis of suspensory ligaments of cooper

questions.answerText: Fibrosis of suspensory ligaments of cooper
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Obstruction of lymphatics of breast

 

The clinical image shows skin dimpling resembling an orange peel texture, also known as peau d’orange, which is a classic sign of breast carcinoma. This condition occurs due to  obstruction of superficial lymphatics

 

Key Features:

 

  1. Peau d’Orange Appearance:
    • Obstruction of lymphatic drainage by tumor cells causes inflammation and edema.
  2. Mechanism:
    • The suspensory ligaments of Cooper connect the breast tissue to the skin.
    • Fibrosis pulls the skin inward, causing dimpling or puckering.

 

Other Options:

 

Option  A. Fibrosis of suspensory ligaments of cooper. It leads to retraction of skin and nipple and is not the main underlying cause for peau d'orange appearance.

 

Option B. Fibrosis of lactiferous glands: This results in nipple retraction but does not cause skin dimpling.

 

Option C. Fibrosis of parenchyma of breast: Not directly related to peau d’orange; this may lead to overall tissue hardening.

 

Educational objective:

 

Peau d’orange appearance in breast carcinoma is caused obstruction of lymphatics

questions.stemHtml: A patient visited with following presentation. Which muscles are paralysed:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) 3rd & 4th lumbricals

 

The image shows a claw hand deformity, which occurs due to paralysis of the 3rd and 4th lumbricals. This deformity is a result of ulnar nerve damage, which innervates the 3rd and 4th lumbricals and the interossei muscles.

 

Key Features:

 

  1. Role of Lumbricals:
    • Lumbricals flex the metacarpophalangeal joints (MCP) and extend the interphalangeal joints (IP).
    • In their absence, there is hyperextension of MCP joints and flexion of IP joints.
  2. Involvement in Claw Hand:
    • Damage to the ulnar nerve affects the 3rd and 4th lumbricals (ulnar innervated).
    • The 1st and 2nd lumbricals, which are innervated by the median nerve, remain unaffected.
  3. Key Differentiation:
    • If all fingers are clawed, both the ulnar and median nerves are involved.
    • In this case, only the ulnar nerve territory (ring and little fingers) is involved, confirming the paralysis of the 3rd and 4th lumbricals.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. 1st & 2nd lumbricals: These are innervated by the median nerve and are not affected here.

 

Option B. 2nd & 3rd lumbricals: Incorrect combination, as these muscles belong to different innervations.

 

Option D. 4th & 5th lumbricals: This numbering does not correspond to actual lumbrical anatomy; lumbricals are numbered from 1st to 4th.

 

Educational objective:

 

Claw hand deformity involving the ring and little fingers is caused by paralysis of the 3rd and 4th lumbricals due to ulnar nerve damage.

questions.stem: A 50-year male Jagan, was presented with severe headache and vomiting and history of immediate unconsciousness immediately. On admission he was found hypertensive and history of poorly controlled hypertension also found. Gradual decline in neurological functions was present. Neck stiffness, Kernig’s sign was also found positive. NCCT was done but it failed to make a diagnosis. Then LP was performed in which CSF was found grossly bloody with RBC counts upto 1 million/cu mm. After 48 hours of clinical manifestations xanthochromic spinal fluid was found. What is your single best diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Subarachnoid haemorrhage

 

The clinical presentation and diagnostic findings strongly indicate subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), primarily caused by the rupture of a berry aneurysm.

 

  1. Key symptoms and signs:
    • Severe headache ("worst headache of life") and vomiting are classic initial symptoms of SAH.
    • Immediate unconsciousness and neurological decline indicate intracranial pressure changes caused by bleeding.
    • Neck stiffness and Kernig’s sign suggest meningeal irritation due to blood in the subarachnoid space.
  2. Diagnostics:
    • NCCT (Non-contrast CT scan): While initial imaging may miss SAH in certain cases, it is the first-line investigation.
    • Lumbar puncture (LP): The finding of grossly bloody CSF with RBCs up to 1 million/cu mm confirms bleeding in the subarachnoid space. The subsequent appearance of xanthochromia after 48 hours is due to the breakdown of RBCs, further confirming SAH.
  3. Etiology:
    • The most common cause of SAH is the rupture of a berry aneurysm within the circle of Willis, often associated with poorly controlled hypertension, as seen in this patient.

 

Other Options: 

 

Option A. Meningitis: Why incorrect: Meningitis can present with neck stiffness and Kernig’s sign; however, it does not cause bloody CSF or xanthochromia. Additionally, meningitis typically features fever and leukocytosis, absent in this case.

 

Option C. Intracerebral hemorrhage: Why incorrect: While intracerebral hemorrhage can occur with poorly controlled hypertension, it does not typically present with bloody CSF or xanthochromia, which are hallmarks of SAH.

 

Option D. Extradural hemorrhage (EDH): Why incorrect: EDH results from trauma and involves bleeding between the skull and dura mater, often presenting with a lucid interval and CT findings of a biconvex hematoma. This scenario lacks such imaging features or trauma history.

 

Note:

 

 

Circle of Willis:

 

  • Major arteries:
    • Anterior cerebral artery (ACA)
    • Middle cerebral artery (MCA)
    • Posterior cerebral artery (PCA)
    • Internal carotid artery (ICA)
    • Anterior and posterior communicating arteries
  • Most common sites for aneurysm rupture:
    • Anterior communicating artery (most common)
    • Posterior communicating artery
    • Bifurcation of MCA

 

Educational objective:

 

Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) is characterized by sudden severe headache, meningeal signs (e.g., neck stiffness), and bloody CSF/xanthochromia due to aneurysmal rupture. Early identification and management are crucial as SAH is a neurosurgical emergency.

questions.stem: A 35 years old alcoholic and chronic smoker male Amit, was having the history of hypercholesterolemia for 8 years. He presented at OPD with hemiplegia on right side of body. On examination he was having loss of proprioception, fine touch and vibration sensations on right side. He was also unable to recognize the objects with closed eyes from right hand. On examination left side of the tongue was atrophied and deviation on left side during protrusion was found. On cerebral angiography there was blockage of artery located in median fissure of spinal cord at lower part of brain stem was found. What is your diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Dejerine’s syndrome (Dejerine’s Anterior Bulbar Syndrome)

 

The vessel present in anterior median fissure of spinal cord is anterior spinal artery.

 

The clinical presentation aligns with medial medullary syndrome (Dejerine’s syndrome), which is caused by damage to structures supplied by the anterior spinal artery at the medullary level.

 

Structures supplied by anterior spinal artery are the paramedian structures of medulla oblongata which include - Pyramidal tract, Hypoglossal nuclei and nerve, Medial Longitudinal fasciculus, tectospinal tract, rubrospinal tract and medial lemniscus.

 

Key Features of Dejerine’s Syndrome:

 

  1. Hemiplegia on the right side of the body:
    • Caused by damage to the corticospinal tract in the medial medulla, which controls motor functions of the contralateral side of the body.
  2. Loss of proprioception, fine touch, and vibration sensations on the right side:
    • Damage to the medial lemniscus, which carries sensory signals (proprioception, vibration, fine touch) from the contralateral side of the body.
  3. Left-sided tongue atrophy and deviation to the left:
    • Indicates involvement of the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII), which emerges from the medial part of the medulla. The atrophy and deviation are ipsilateral due to lower motor neuron damage.

 

Anatomy:

 

  • The medial part of the medulla (affected in this case) contains:
    • Hypoglossal nucleus (CN XII): Tongue motor control.
    • Corticospinal tract: Motor pathways for the contralateral body.
    • Medial lemniscus: Sensory pathway for proprioception, fine touch, and vibration.
  • The anterior spinal artery supplies this region, and its occlusion leads to Dejerine’s syndrome.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Perinaud’s Syndrome: A midbrain syndrome characterized by vertical gaze palsy due to compression of the dorsal midbrain, usually caused by pineal tumors or hydrocephalus. Not related to medullary damage.

 

Option B. Benedikt’s Syndrome: Another midbrain syndrome, involving the red nucleus, causing contralateral ataxia and tremor along with oculomotor nerve palsy. The presentation does not match.

 

Option D. Wallenberg Syndrome: This is the lateral medullary syndrome, caused by occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA). Symptoms include dysphagia, hoarseness (CN X), ipsilateral Horner’s syndrome, and contralateral pain/temperature loss. No involvement of CN XII or medial structures. or medial structures.

 

Educational objective:

 

Dejerine’s Syndrome (Medial Medullary Syndrome) is caused by blockage of the anterior spinal artery at the medulla, leading to:

 

  1. Contralateral hemiplegia (corticospinal tract damage).
  2. Contralateral loss of proprioception and vibration (medial lemniscus damage).
  3. Ipsilateral tongue atrophy and deviation (CN XII damage).

questions.stem: Which nerve is cut in Vidian’s Neurectomy?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Nerve in Pterygoid canal 

 

The nerve of the pterygoid canal, also known as Vidian's nerve, is the nerve targeted during Vidian's neurectomy. Vidian’s neurectomy is a surgical procedure primarily performed for the management of allergic rhinitis or vasomotor rhinitis when medical treatment, such as antihistamines and steroids, is insufficient.

 

The Vidian nerve is formed by the confluence of two nerves:

 

  • Greater superficial petrosal nerve, which is a branch of the facial nerve carrying parasympathetic fibers.
  • Deep petrosal nerve, which originates from the sympathetic plexus around the internal carotid artery.

 

These two nerves merge in the pterygoid canal to form the nerve of the pterygoid canal (Vidian nerve), which supplies the lacrimal gland, nasal glands, and palatine glands. Cutting this nerve interrupts the parasympathetic and sympathetic nerve supply, reducing glandular secretions and alleviating rhinitis symptoms.

 

Key Facts:

 

  • The procedure involves a small incision to cut the nerve in the pterygoid canal, which is located near the palatine ganglion.
  • The Vidian nerve plays a role in glandular secretion, so its neurectomy reduces nasal and palatine gland activity.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Nerve in Inferior orbital fissure: The nerve passing through the inferior orbital fissure is the infraorbital nerve, a branch of the maxillary nerve (V2). This nerve is unrelated to Vidian’s neurectomy.

 

Option B. Nerve in Incisive foramen: The nasopalatine nerve, a branch of the maxillary nerve, passes through the incisive foramen. This nerve is involved in innervation of the anterior palate, not related to the pterygoid canal or Vidian nerve.

 

Option C. Nerve in Tympanomastoid fissure: The nerve exiting through the tympanomastoid fissure is the auricular branch of the vagus nerve (Arnold's nerve), which is unrelated to Vidian’s neurectomy.

 

Educational objective:

 

The nerve of the pterygoid canal (Vidian nerve) is the target in Vidian’s neurectomy, a procedure performed for refractory cases of allergic or vasomotor rhinitis by reducing glandular secretions. It is formed by the union of the greater superficial petrosal nerve and deep petrosal nerve.

questions.stemHtml: In given MRI image identify the marked structure?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Arbor Vitae 


The marked structure in the MRI image is the Arbor Vitae, a tree-like white matter arrangement found within the cerebellum. The Arbor Vitae, which means "tree of life," is responsible for coordinating motor activities and processing sensory input to ensure balance and fine motor control. It is part of the cerebellar anatomy and plays a critical role in maintaining proper movement and coordination.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Hypothalamus: The hypothalamus is located inferior to the thalamus and is part of the diencephalon, primarily involved in homeostasis and hormonal control, not coordination.

 

Option B. thalamus: the thalamus serves as a relay station for sensory and motor signals to the cerebral cortex, but it does not exhibit the tree-like structure seen in the image.

 

Option D. Master of Orchestra: This term is metaphorical and not an anatomical structure; it does not exist as a labeled part of the brain.

 

Educational Objective:


The Arbor Vitae is the tree-like white matter structure within the cerebellum responsible for motor coordination and balance.

questions.stemHtml: During orthopaedic surgery tendon was required in lower limb. Which muscle is used for tendon grafting operation in lower limb surgery?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) A

 

The plantaris muscle (marked as A) is often used in orthopedic surgeries for tendon grafting operations in the lower limb. This muscle has a short belly and an extremely long tendon, which makes it an ideal choice for grafting without significant functional loss.

 

Key Features of the Plantaris Muscle:

 

  1. Anatomy: The plantaris is a small, vestigial muscle located in the posterior compartment of the leg. It lies superficial to the soleus and deep to the gastrocnemius.
  2. Tendon Characteristics: The plantaris tendon is long, slender, and strong, making it suitable for reconstruction procedures.
  3. Clinical Use:
    • Tendon grafts for repairing ligaments (e.g., ACL reconstruction).
    • Tendon transfer surgeries in the lower limb.
  4. Functional Loss: The plantaris is considered vestigial in humans, so its removal has negligible impact on function.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. B: Represents the soleus, a deeper and more powerful muscle involved in plantarflexion. Its tendon is part of the Achilles tendon but is not typically used for grafting due to its importance in locomotion.

 

Option C. C: Represents the gastrocnemius, a large superficial calf muscle with medial and lateral heads. Its tendon merges into the Achilles tendon and is critical for plantarflexion and walking.

 

Option D. D: Represents the Achilles tendon itself, the strongest tendon in the body, which is essential for powerful movements like jumping and running. It is not removed for grafting.

 

Educational objective:

 

The plantaris muscle is commonly used for tendon grafting in orthopedic surgeries due to its long tendon, which can be harvested without significant functional loss. It is marked as A in the image.

questions.stem: A patient age 45 presented with difficulty in foot eversion and sensory loss on the lateral leg & dorsum of foot. The nerve injured is?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Superficial peroneal nerve

 

The superficial peroneal nerve is the primary nerve responsible for supplying the muscles of the lateral compartment of the leg, including the peroneus longus and peroneus brevis. These muscles are involved in foot eversion. Additionally, the nerve provides sensory innervation to the lateral leg and the dorsum of the foot, excluding the first interdigital cleft, which is supplied by the deep peroneal nerve.

 

 

In this case, the patient presented with:

 

  • Difficulty in foot eversion: This indicates paralysis of the lateral compartment muscles, namely peroneus longus and brevis. These muscles are innervated by the superficial peroneal nerve.
  • Sensory loss on the lateral leg and dorsum of the foot: This sensory distribution matches the area supplied by the superficial peroneal nerve.

 

These clinical signs point to an injury of the superficial peroneal nerve.

 

Other Options:

 

  1. Deep peroneal nerve
    • Why incorrect: The deep peroneal nerve innervates the anterior compartment of the leg, responsible for dorsiflexion of the foot and extension of the toes. It also provides sensory innervation to the first interdigital cleft, not the lateral leg or dorsum of the foot. Hence, the symptoms described do not align with a deep peroneal nerve injury.
  2. Sural nerve
    • Why incorrect: The sural nerve provides sensory innervation to the posterior aspect of the lower leg and the lateral foot, but it does not innervate muscles responsible for foot eversion. This nerve injury would not cause motor deficits related to eversion.
  3. Saphenous nerve
    • Why incorrect: The saphenous nerve is a purely sensory nerve supplying the medial aspect of the lower leg. It has no role in motor functions or sensation of the lateral leg or dorsum of the foot, making it irrelevant to the symptoms presented.

 

Educational objective:

 

The superficial peroneal nerve supplies the muscles of the lateral compartment of the leg (peroneus longus and brevis) responsible for foot eversion and provides sensory innervation to the lateral leg and dorsum of the foot.

questions.stem: A 67 year old lady Janki, presented with loss of subconscious kinaesthetic sensation, loss of pain and temperature sensation as well as loss of crude touch from body. On examination fine touch sensation was found normal. In case of spinal angiography blockage of which of the following artery might be seen?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Anterior spinal artery

 

The anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord, including the tracts responsible for subconscious kinesthetic sensation, pain and temperature sensation, and crude touch. 

 

 

 

 

  1. Subconscious kinesthetic sensation is carried by the dorsal spinocerebellar and ventral spinocerebellar tracts, both located in the lateral portion of the spinal cord and supplied by the anterior spinal artery.
  2. Pain and temperature sensation is carried by the lateral spinothalamic tract, which lies in the lateral white matter of the spinal cord and also depends on the anterior spinal artery for its blood supply.
  3. Crude touch is transmitted via the anterior spinothalamic tract, located in the anterior spinal cord and again within the territory of the anterior spinal artery.
  4. Fine touch sensation, which was preserved in this case, is carried by the fasciculus gracilis and fasciculus cuneatus in the posterior column. These tracts are supplied by the posterior spinal artery, which remained intact in this patient.

 

Given the loss of functions corresponding to the anterior spinal artery territory and the sparing of functions supplied by the posterior spinal artery, the likely site of arterial blockage is the anterior spinal artery.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Posterior spinal artery: Why incorrect: This artery supplies the posterior one-third of the spinal cord, including the dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis and fasciculus cuneatus), which are responsible for fine touch, proprioception, and vibration sense. Since these functions are normal in this patient, the posterior spinal artery is not involved.

 

Option C. Anterior inferior cerebellar artery: Why incorrect: This artery supplies part of the cerebellum and the brainstem. It does not supply the spinal cord, so it is not relevant to the clinical presentation.

 

Option D. Posterior inferior cerebellar artery: Why incorrect: Similar to the anterior inferior cerebellar artery, this artery supplies parts of the cerebellum and brainstem, not the spinal cord. Therefore, its blockage would not result in the described spinal cord symptoms.

 

Educational objective:

 

The anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord, including the tracts for pain and temperature sensation, crude touch, and subconscious kinesthetic sensation. Blockage of this artery results in anterior spinal artery syndrome, characterized by the loss of these sensations while sparing fine touch and proprioception.

questions.stem: A 40 years old female Vimla, presented with road traffic accident with brief loss of consciousness. Fatigue, pallor and weakness on general examination. She was also having mild jaundice and gall stones. Massive hepatosplenomegaly with hypersplenism was also found. On skull radiography widening of diploic spaces was found. On previous history she was reported to had failure to thrive in early childhood, growth retardation, delayed puberty. Other findings are leg ulcer and skin bronzing. After the RTA she is having headache and also presenting with lucid interval, nausea, vomiting focal neurological deficits. On plain X ray skull fracture is visible and on CT scan hyperdense biconvex opacity is visible on temporal region. What is your single best diagnosis for current presentation?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Extradural haemorrhage

The patient presents with a history of trauma and subsequent neurological symptoms including a lucid interval, a hallmark feature of extradural hemorrhage (EDH). On CT, a hyperdense biconvex (lens-shaped) opacity in the temporal region is diagnostic of EDH, commonly associated with trauma leading to rupture of the middle meningeal artery.

 

  • Mechanism of EDH: The middle meningeal artery runs outside the dura mater, and fractures in the temporal bone can rupture it. Blood accumulates between the skull and dura mater, leading to a lens-shaped opacity on imaging. The lucid interval occurs as initial recovery after trauma is followed by a progressive neurological decline due to hematoma expansion.

 

 

 

While the patient has a history of thalassemia, indicated by fatigue, pallor, jaundice, gallstones, hepatosplenomegaly, and skeletal abnormalities (chipmunk facies, widened diploic spaces), her current presentation is primarily explained by EDH due to the RTA. 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Thalassemia: incorrect: The patient has a clear history and clinical features consistent with thalassemia, including chronic anemia, hepatosplenomegaly, and bone deformities. However, the acute neurological symptoms, lucid interval, and CT findings point to EDH as the primary diagnosis in this scenario.

 

Option B. Migraine: incorrect: Migraine typically presents with episodic headaches often associated with aura, nausea, or photophobia. It does not cause focal neurological deficits, lucid intervals, or the radiological findings described here.

 

Option C. Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH): incorrect: SAH often presents with a sudden "thunderclap headache," nausea, vomiting, and altered consciousness. On imaging, it appears as hyperdensity in the sulci or basal cisterns. The biconvex opacity seen in this case is not characteristic of SAH.

 

Educational objective:

 

Extradural hemorrhage (EDH) is characterized by a lucid interval following trauma, commonly caused by rupture of the middle meningeal artery. On CT, it appears as a hyperdense biconvex (lens-shaped) opacity, often located in the temporal region. This condition is a neurosurgical emergency.

questions.stem: A patient Ramlal, 56 years old male, presented with history of palanaesthesia, astereognosis, loss of proprioception and fine touch sensation. He has chronic history of smoking, diabetes and hypertension. In case of spinal angiography blockage of which of the following artery might be seen:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Posterior spinal artery 

 

The clinical presentation indicates a posterior spinal artery syndrome, characterized by the loss of functions mediated by the dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis and fasciculus cuneatus):

 

  1. Fine touch sensation: Carried by the dorsal column medial lemniscus pathway.
  2. Proprioception: Awareness of limb position, also carried by the dorsal columns.
  3. Pallanaesthesia: Loss of vibration sense, mediated by the dorsal columns.
  4. Astereognosis: Inability to recognize objects by touch, another function of the dorsal  columns.

 

 

 

The posterior spinal arteries supply the posterior one-third of the spinal cord, including the fasciculus gracilis and fasciculus cuneatus, which are responsible for these sensory modalities. Chronic conditions such as smoking, diabetes, and hypertension increase the risk of atherosclerosis, which may result in arterial blockage.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Anterior spinal artery: incorrect: The anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord, including the lateral corticospinal tract, spinothalamic tracts, and ventral horns. Blockage would lead to anterior spinal artery syndrome, with motor deficits, pain, and temperature loss, not the sensory deficits described here.

 

Option C. Anterior inferior cerebellar artery: incorrect: This artery supplies the lower pons and parts of the cerebellum. Blockage would not cause isolated dorsal column symptoms or spinal cord-specific issues.

 

Option D. Posterior inferior cerebellar artery:  incorrect: This artery supplies the cerebellum and the medulla. Blockage would lead to Wallenberg syndrome (lateral medullary syndrome), characterized by symptoms like vertigo, ataxia, and contralateral pain and temperature sensation loss, none of which are present here.

 

Educational objective:

 

The posterior spinal artery supplies the dorsal columns of the spinal cord, responsible for fine touch, proprioception, vibration, and stereognosis. Blockage of this artery causes posterior spinal artery syndrome, leading to loss of these specific sensory modalities without motor or pain/temperature deficits.

questions.stem: In adults, lumbar puncture is done at?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) L3-L4

 

In adults, lumbar puncture is typically performed at the L3-L4 or L4-L5 interspace. These levels are chosen because the spinal cord in adults usually ends at the level of L1-L2, and the lumbar cistern (subarachnoid space containing CSF) extends down to S2. Performing the procedure below the termination of the spinal cord minimizes the risk of spinal cord injury.

 

  • L3-L4 interspace is preferred in adults as it is easily located using the Tuffier’s line (an imaginary line drawn between the highest points of the iliac crests, which intersects the L4 vertebral body).
  • L4-L5: While commonly used in children, this level is also a safe alternative in adults if necessary.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In adults, lumbar puncture is most commonly performed at the L3-L4 interspace, ensuring safety by accessing the lumbar cistern below the termination of the spinal cord.

questions.stem: A 45 years old alcoholic and chronic smoker male was having the history of hypercholesterolemia for 12 years. He presented at OPD with hemiplegia on right side of body. Also tremor, hypokinesia and rigidity was found on right side of body. On examination drooping eyelid and fixed wide pupil pointed down and out leading to diplopia found. On cerebral angiography occlusion of paramedian branches of posterior cerebral artery was found. What is your diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Weber syndrome 

 

Weber syndrome, also known as medial midbrain syndrome, is caused by an infarction in the paramedian branches of the posterior cerebral artery, leading to damage in the medial part of the midbrain. The key features in this case align with Weber syndrome:

 

  1. Third Cranial Nerve Palsy (Oculomotor Nerve):
    • Results in:
      • Squint
      • Ptosis (drooping eyelid)
      • Fixed, dilated pupil (due to unopposed sympathetic activity)
      • Eye deviated down and out (unopposed action of lateral rectus and superior oblique muscles)
      • Causes diplopia
  2. Contralateral Hemiplegia:
    • Caused by damage to the corticospinal tract in the cerebral peduncle, leading to weakness or paralysis of the opposite side of the body.
    • Contralateral paralysis of lower half of face and tongue due to involvement of corticobulbar tract
  3. Extrapyramidal Symptoms:
    • Tremor, hypokinesia, and rigidity result from involvement of the substantia nigra, which is part of the extrapyramidal system and closely related to the midbrain structures.
    • Tremors are the main features of benedikt syndrome but can be seen in any lesion of midbrain which is involving the substantia nigra.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Perinaud’s Syndrome incorrect: This syndrome results from lesions in the dorsal midbrain (superior colliculus, pretectal area), often due to pineal gland tumors. It presents with vertical gaze palsy and light-near dissociation, which are absent here.

 

Option B. Benedikt’s Syndrome

 

  • incorrect: Benedikt’s syndrome involves the tegmentum of the midbrain, leading to:
    • Third nerve palsy (like in Weber syndrome)
    • Contralateral ataxia and tremor (due to damage to the red nucleus and cerebellar pathways).
    • While the third nerve involvement is common, the extrapyramidal symptoms in Benedikt’s syndrome are more cerebellar (ataxia), whereas rigidity and tremor in Weber syndrome result from nigrostriatal involvement.

 

Option D. Facial Colliculus Syndrome incorrect: This is a pons-related syndrome, involving the facial and abducens nuclei. It causes ipsilateral facial paralysis and an inability to abduct the eye, which are not seen in this case.

 

Mnemonic to Remember Midbrain Syndromes:

 

Three Midbrain Syndromes:

 

  1. P for Perinaud’s Syndrome:
    • Pineal gland tumor
    • Posterior midbrain
    • Vertical gaze palsy
  2. B for Benedikt’s Syndrome:
    • Between structures of the midbrain (tegmentum)
    • Third nerve palsy + Ataxia, Tremor (red nucleus involvement)
  3. W for Weber Syndrome:
    • White matter (cerebral peduncle)
    • Third nerve palsy + Hemiplegia (corticospinal tract involvement)

 

Educational objective:

 

Weber Syndrome is caused by infarction of the paramedian branches of the posterior cerebral artery, leading to:

 

  • Oculomotor nerve palsy
  • Contralateral hemiplegia
  • Extrapyramidal symptoms due to nigrostriatal pathway involvement.

questions.stem: Handle bar palsy occurs due to compression of which nerve?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Ulnar nerve 

 

Handlebar palsy is a condition caused by prolonged compression of the ulnar nerve at the wrist or palm. This commonly occurs during activities such as cycling when the hand rests on the handlebars, leading to nerve compression in Guyon's canal.

 

  1. Anatomy of Ulnar Nerve:
    • The ulnar nerve runs through Guyon's canal (a tunnel formed by the pisiform and hamate bones in the wrist).
    • It supplies:
      • Motor branches: To intrinsic hand muscles, except the thenar muscles and the first two lumbricals.
      • Sensory branches: To the medial one and a half fingers (little finger and half of the ring finger).
  2. Clinical Features of Handlebar Palsy:
    • Motor symptoms:
      • Weakness of hand grip.
      • Difficulty in finger abduction and adduction.
    • Sensory symptoms:
      • Numbness or tingling in the medial one and a half fingers.
    • Prolonged compression can lead to ulnar claw hand, characterized by hyperextension of the metacarpophalangeal joints and flexion of the interphalangeal joints of the fourth and fifth fingers.

 

Other Options:

 

  1. Median nerve:
    • Compression leads to carpal tunnel syndrome, characterized by numbness in the lateral three and a half fingers and weakness in the thenar muscles.
    • Not associated with handlebar palsy.
  2. Radial nerve:
    • Compression typically occurs in the arm or forearm, causing wrist drop due to weakness in wrist and finger extensors.
    • It does not pass through Guyon's canal or supply the medial hand.
  3. Axillary nerve:
    • Supplies the deltoid and teres minor muscles and provides sensation to the lateral shoulder.
    • Not involved in hand or wrist symptoms.

 

Educational objective:

 

Handlebar palsy results from prolonged compression of the ulnar nerve at the wrist, often in Guyon's canal, leading to sensory and motor deficits in the medial hand and fingers.

questions.stemHtml: On ENT examination tympanic membrane was seen as given image. Identify the marked structure?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Chorda tympani

 

The tympanic membrane, also known as the eardrum, is a thin, pearly white membrane that separates the external ear from the middle ear. In the provided image, the marked structure passing across the tympanic membrane is identified as the chorda tympani nerve.

 

The chorda tympani is a branch of the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) that traverses through the middle ear. It runs between the malleus and the incus as it crosses the tympanic cavity, eventually exiting the skull to join the lingual nerve. It carries taste sensations from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and parasympathetic fibers to the submandibular and sublingual glands.

 

Key observations supporting the identification:

 

  • The pearly white membrane is clearly visible, with the handle of the malleus as a prominent structure.
  • The marked structure, identified as chorda tympani, crosses horizontally over the tympanic membrane.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Incus: The incus is a middle ear ossicle and does not appear as a thin cord-like structure crossing the tympanic membrane. Instead, it articulates with the malleus and stapes.

 

Option C. Stapes: The stapes is another ossicle of the middle ear, located further medially and connected to the oval window. It does not cross the tympanic membrane.

 

Option D. Malleus: The handle of the malleus is visible as a vertical structure attached to the tympanic membrane, ending at the umbo. It does not resemble the thin horizontal structure marked in the image.

 

Note:

 

  • The incudomalleolar joint is a saddle joint.
  • The incudostapedial joint is a ball-and-socket joint.

 

Educational objective:

 

The chorda tympani nerve is a branch of the facial nerve that runs through the middle ear, crossing the tympanic membrane between the malleus and the incus. It plays a role in taste sensation and parasympathetic innervation to salivary glands.

questions.stemHtml: Blockage of artery supplying to indicate area will cause all except?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Ataxia 

 

Ataxia is caused by dysfunction of the cerebellum or its connections, not by damage to the paracentral lobule or its arterial supply.


The indicated area in the image is the paracentral lobule, located on the medial surface of the cerebral cortex. The paracentral lobule is responsible for motor and sensory innervation of the lower extremities, perineum, and pelvic floor. Blockage of the arterial supply to this area, such as the anterior cerebral artery (ACA), can result in rectal and urinary incontinence, as well as perianal anesthesia, due to loss of sensory and motor control of the corresponding regions. 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Rectal incontinence: The paracentral lobule controls motor activity of the pelvic floor, and arterial blockage can lead to rectal incontinence due to loss of motor control.

 

Option B. Urinary incontinence: Damage to this area affects motor control of the urinary sphincter, leading to urinary incontinence.

 

Option C. Perianal anaesthesia: Loss of sensory innervation to the perianal region occurs due to disruption in the sensory fibers controlled by the paracentral lobule.

 

Educational Objective:


Blockage of the anterior cerebral artery supplying the paracentral lobule can cause rectal and urinary incontinence and perianal anesthesia, but ataxia is not associated with this lesion.

The ulnar nerve is located at the medial epicondyle of the humerus, marked as site D in the image. questions.stemHtml: Structure palpated in deltopectoral groove?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) B 

 

The deltopectoral groove is the anatomical groove formed between the deltoid muscle and the pectoralis major muscle. It is a landmark region where the cephalic vein is located and can be palpated. The structure labeled B in the image corresponds to the coracoid process, which is also palpated in this region.

 

The cephalic vein passes just under the coracoid process

 

Key Features of the Deltopectoral Groove:

 

  1. The groove is located anteriorly between the deltoid and pectoralis major muscles.
  2. Palpable structures include:
    • Cephalic vein: A superficial vein frequently used for cannulation.
    • Coracoid process: A bony prominence of the scapula, which serves as an attachment for various ligaments and muscles such as the short head of the biceps brachii and coracobrachialis.

 

The coracoid process is easily identified in the deltopectoral groove as a hard bony structure just inferior to the lateral end of the clavicle.

 

Other structures marked are:


A - Acromion process


C- Spine of scapula


D - Glenoid cavity

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. A: This structure is not located in the deltopectoral groove. It may correspond to the acromion process, which is a bony prominence at the superior aspect of the scapula.

 

Option C. C: This structure is unrelated to the groove and may correspond to the lateral end of the clavicle or another scapular process.

 

Option D. D: This represents the shaft of the humerus and is not a structure palpable in the deltopectoral groove.

 

Educational objective:

 

The coracoid process, labeled B in the image, is the key bony structure palpated in the deltopectoral groove, along with the cephalic vein. It is an important landmark for clinicians during shoulder procedures and physical examinations.

questions.stemHtml: Given image is 3 dimensional CT imaging of arterial supply of lower limb. Identify the posterior tibial artery?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) D

 

The posterior tibial artery is a key artery in the lower limb that runs posterior to the medial malleolus and supplies blood to the posterior compartment of the leg and plantar surface of the foot.

 

Key Features of the Posterior Tibial Artery:

 

  1. Origin: It is a terminal branch of the popliteal artery.
  2. Course:
    • Travels along the posterior compartment of the leg.
    • Runs posterior to the medial malleolus and into the foot, where it forms the medial and lateral plantar arteries.
  3. Identification in Image: In the given CT image:
    • The artery labeled D is located in the posterior compartment, making it the posterior tibial artery.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. A: Represents the common iliac artery, which gives rise to the external and internal iliac arteries.

 

Option B. B: Indicates the femoral artery, a continuation of the external iliac artery after passing under the inguinal ligament.

 

Option C. C: Represents the popliteal artery, which is the continuation of the femoral artery behind the knee.

 

Educational objective:

 

The posterior tibial artery (labeled D) is a major branch of the popliteal artery that supplies the posterior compartment of the leg and plantar surface of the foot. It is critical for vascular supply in the lower limb.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the long head of biceps?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) C

 

The image shows a section of shoulder joint.

 

The long head of the biceps brachii originates from the supraglenoid tubercle of the scapula, located above the glenoid cavity. This muscle runs through the shoulder joint and continues along the intertubercular (bicipital) groove of the humerus.

 

Key Points:

 

  • The long head of the biceps crosses both the shoulder and elbow joints, contributing to shoulder stabilization and elbow flexion.
  • Its anatomical position above the glenoid cavity (supraglenoid tubercle) distinguishes it from the short head of the biceps, which originates from the coracoid process.

 

Other Options:

Option D. D: Represents the short head of biceps brachii which is taking origin from the coracoid process.

 

Educational objective:

 

The long head of the biceps brachii originates from the supraglenoid tubercle of the scapula (labeled C), while the short head originates from the coracoid process.

The flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) is the most bulky and powerful muscle on the front of forearm and provides main gripping power to the hand.
 

Origin:

questions.answerText: Infection of hand & forearm space of Parona
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Infection of hand & forearm space of Parona

 

Hourglass stenosis refers to a condition where there is swelling and narrowing in the infected area, creating an "hourglass" appearance. This is often seen in infections involving the hand that spread to the forearm space of Parona.

 

  • The forearm space of Parona is located between the deep flexor tendons of the forearm and the pronator quadratus muscle.
  • Infection in this space may spread from the hand, particularly through the radial bursa (associated with the thumb) or ulnar bursa (associated with the little finger).
  • Swelling in both the hand and the forearm, combined with the narrow area between them, results in the characteristic hourglass appearance.

 

This is typically observed in severe infections, such as tenosynovitis, originating from puncture wounds or poorly managed hand infections.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Infection of thenar space: Infections in the thenar space involve the thumb area but do not typically spread to the forearm space of Parona, hence they do not result in hourglass stenosis.

 

Option C. Infection of hypothenar space & thenar space: While infections in these spaces can involve hand swelling, they do not directly spread to the forearm space, making this option incorrect.

 

Option D. Infection of pulp space: This involves localized infections in the distal phalanx (e.g., felons) and does not spread proximally to cause hourglass stenosis.

 

Educational objective:

 

Hourglass stenosis is a clinical condition characterized by swelling in the hand and the forearm space of Parona, connected by a narrowed region. This is commonly seen in infections that spread through the bursae of the hand.

questions.stemHtml: One chronic alcoholic patient was diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis. His presented with following clinical condition: What is your diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Dupuytren’s contracture 

 

The image shows Dupuytren’s contracture, a condition characterized by progressive fibrosis of the palmar aponeurosis, leading to flexion deformities in the fingers, most commonly the ring and little fingers.

 

Key Features of Dupuytren’s Contracture:

 

  1. Pathology:
    • Fibrosis and thickening of the palmar aponeurosis.
    • Formation of nodules and cords, progressing to finger contractures.
  2. Stages:
    • Grade 1: Formation of nodules in the palm.
    • Grade 2: Formation of fibrous cords extending to the fingers.
    • Grade 3: Permanent flexion deformity of fingers.
  3. Risk Factors:
    • Chronic alcoholism.
    • Rheumatoid arthritis and other connective tissue disorders.
    • Genetic predisposition.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Ulnar claw hand: Results from ulnar nerve damage, affecting the 3rd and 4th lumbricals, causing clawing of the ring and little fingers. Not related to palmar aponeurosis fibrosis.

 

Option B. Benedict hand deformity: Seen in median nerve damage, where the patient cannot flex the index and middle fingers.

 

Option D. Carpal tunnel syndrome: Involves median nerve compression, causing tingling and numbness in the thumb, index, and middle fingers, unrelated to finger contractures.

 

Educational objective:

 

Dupuytren’s contracture is a progressive fibrotic condition of the palmar aponeurosis, leading to nodules, cords, and flexion deformities in the fingers. It is associated with chronic alcoholism and connective tissue disorders.

questions.stem: Grave yard of ulnar nerve is?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Adductor pollicis

 

The adductor pollicis muscle is known as the "graveyard of the ulnar nerve" because it is the final muscle to receive motor innervation from the ulnar nerve before the nerve terminates. The ulnar nerve provides motor innervation to this muscle via its deep branch.

 

  • The adductor pollicis is located in the thenar compartment of the hand and is responsible for adduction of the thumb.
  • The ulnar nerve travels through Guyon's canal (ulnar tunnel) in the wrist, and compression of the nerve in this canal can lead to weakness or paralysis of the adductor pollicis muscle, along with other intrinsic hand muscles.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Abductor pollicis longus: This muscle is located in the posterior forearm and is innervated by the radial nerve. It is unrelated to the ulnar nerve.

 

Option C. Extensor pollicis longus: This is also a forearm muscle, responsible for thumb extension, and is innervated by the radial nerve.

 

Option D. Extensor pollicis brevis: Like the extensor pollicis longus, this muscle is innervated by the radial nerve and is unrelated to the ulnar nerve.

 

Educational objective:

 

The adductor pollicis is referred to as the "graveyard of the ulnar nerve" because it is the last muscle supplied by the ulnar nerve. It plays a critical role in thumb adduction and is often assessed to evaluate ulnar nerve function.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the vertebra?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) C1

 

The vertebra shown in the image is C1, also known as the atlas. The atlas is the first cervical vertebra and has a distinctive structure that differentiates it from other cervical vertebrae:

 

  1. Unique Features of C1 (Atlas):
    • No vertebral body: Instead, it has an anterior arch.
    • No spinous process: It has a posterior arch.
    • Large vertebral foramen: This allows for the passage of the spinal cord.
    • Superior articular facets: These are concave and articulate with the occipital condyles of the skull to form the atlanto-occipital joint.
    • Foramen transversarium: Present on each transverse process, characteristic of all cervical vertebrae.
  2. These features allow the atlas to support the skull and facilitate the "yes" nodding movement of the head.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. C2 (Axis): The axis has a prominent dens (odontoid process) that serves as a pivot for the rotation of the atlas, which is not seen in the image.

 

Option C. C3 and D. C4: These vertebrae are typical cervical vertebrae with a vertebral body, spinous process, and smaller vertebral foramen. They do not match the structure shown.

 

Educational objective:

 

The C1 vertebra (Atlas) lacks a body and spinous process, has a large vertebral foramen, and is specialized for supporting the skull and facilitating head movements.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the Honeymoon muscle?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) A

 

The honeymoon muscle is the sartorius muscle, which is the longest muscle in the body. It is called the honeymoon muscle because of its role in abduction of the hip, which opens the genital region, aiding in sexual intercourse.

 

Key Features of the Sartorius Muscle:

 

  1. Origin: Anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS).
  2. Insertion: Medial aspect of the proximal tibia, contributing to the pes anserinus.
  3. Actions:
    • Flexion of the hip.
    • Abduction of the hip.
    • Lateral rotation of the femur.
    • Flexion of the knee.
  4. The combination of these actions helps in assuming a cross-legged sitting position, hence the name Taylor’s muscle.

 

In the image, A marks the sartorius muscle, confirming it as the honeymoon muscle.

 

It is supplied by Anterior division of femoral nerve.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. B: This indicates the rectus femoris, a bipennate muscle of the quadriceps group responsible for flexion of the hip and extension of the knee.

Option C. C: This is the vastus lateralis, another muscle of the 

quadriceps group. It is commonly used for intramuscular injections, particularly in pediatric patients.

 

Option D. D: This represents the gracilis, a medial compartment muscle involved in adduction of the thigh. It is also known as the "anti-rape muscle" or "custodian of virginity" because of its role in closing the thighs. It is supplied by Obturator nerve

questions.stem: Which nerve is known as pregnant nerve?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Both

 

A pregnant nerve refers to a nerve that is thick and has an artery running within it to supply it with nutrients, resembling a "pregnant" state. Both the optic nerve and the sciatic nerve fit this description due to their structure and associated arteries.

 

Key Features:

 

  • Optic Nerve:
    • The optic nerve (Cranial Nerve II) is a thick nerve associated with vision.
    • Ophthalmic artery runs along with it in the initial phase; later on, the branch of ophthalmic artery, i.e., the retinal artery runs along the ophthalmic artery.
    • This artery is a classical example of an end artery, meaning its blockage can lead to significant vision loss.
  • Sciatic Nerve:
    • The sciatic nerve is the thickest nerve in the body, supplying the lower limb.
    • It contains an arterial supply through branches of the inferior gluteal artery, which run within the nerve to nourish its large structure.
  • Conclusion:
    • Both the optic and sciatic nerves are thick and contain arteries running within them, meeting the criteria for a "pregnant nerve."

questions.stem: For syringomyelia which of the following statement is false:

options.label: A
options.text: It is related with Dissociative anaesthesia

options.label: B
options.text: Loss of pain and temperature sensations but crude and fine touch sensations remain normal

options.label: C
options.text: Loss of pain, temperature and crude touch sensations and fine touch sensation remains normal

options.label: D
options.text: One of the cause is syphilis

questions.answerText: Loss of pain and temperature sensations but crude and fine touch sensations remain normal
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B. Loss of pain and temperature sensations but crude but  fine touch sensations remain normal

 

Syringomyelia is the neurological condition in which there is development of fluid filled cyst (or syrinx) near the central canal of the spinal cord. 
 

Crude touch, temperature and pain sensations are carried by spinothalamic tracts (anterior & lateral). Hence these are affected. 
 

Whereas fine touch is carried by the fasciculus cuneatus and gracilis which is present in the posterior column of the spinal cord hence they are not affected. 

 

 

Key Features of Syringomyelia:

 

Dissociative Anesthesia:

 

  • Loss of pain and temperature sensation, while touch sensation (both fine and crude) remains intact.
    • The lateral spinothalamic tract is affected, as it crosses near the central canal, while the anterior spinothalamic tract and dorsal columns remain unaffected.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. It is associated with dissociative anesthesia, as explained above.

 

Option C. Pain and temperature sensations are lost, along with crude touch.

 

Option D. One of the causes of syringomyelia is syphilis, which can lead to spinal cord degeneration and cavity formation.

 

Educational objective:

 

In syringomyelia, there is loss of pain and temperature sensation due to the involvement of the lateral spinothalamic tract, crude but fine touch sensations remain intact. The false statement is B.

questions.stem: Tracts are defined as bundle of axons with similar:

options.label: A
options.text: Origin, course, termination but function is different

options.label: B
options.text: Origin, course, function but termination is different

options.label: C
options.text: Origin, termination, function but course is different

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Origin, course, termination, function 

 

A tract is defined as a bundle of axons within the central nervous system (CNS) that share similar characteristics, including:

 

  1. Origin: The location where the axons originate (e.g., specific neurons or nuclei).
  2. Course: The pathway or route taken by the axons through the CNS.
  3. Termination: The destination or structure where the axons synapse or end.
  4. Function: The specific role or type of signal (e.g., motor, sensory, or autonomic) conveyed by the axons.

 

For example:

 

  • The corticospinal tract originates in the cerebral cortex, courses through the brainstem and spinal cord, terminates in the spinal motor neurons, and serves the function of voluntary motor control.

 

 

Key Points:

 

  • Axonal bundles are referred to as tracts in the CNS and have highly specific and consistent properties.
  • The nucleus is a collection of neuronal cell bodies within the CNS, while axons within the PNS form nerves.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Origin, course, termination but function is different: This is incorrect, as function must also be the same in a tract.

 

Option B. Origin, course, function but termination is different: This is incorrect, as the termination is a defining feature of a tract.

 

Option C. Origin, termination, function but course is different: This is incorrect, as the course must also be consistent in a tract.

 

Educational objective:

 

A tract is a bundle of axons in the CNS that shares the same origin, course, termination, and function. This strict definition ensures specificity in neural communication pathways. The correct answer is D.

questions.stemHtml: In shown clinical disease which of the following cells are damaged in Spinal cord:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Ventral horn cells 

 

The clinical image indicates poliomyelitis, a disease caused by the poliovirus, which primarily affects the ventral horn cells (also called anterior horn cells) in the spinal cord. These cells are responsible for motor functions, and their damage leads to flaccid paralysis and muscle atrophy.

 

Key Features of Poliomyelitis:

 

  1. Pathology:
    • Poliovirus selectively damages ventral horn cells, which house motor neurons.
    • This results in lower motor neuron (LMN) lesions, leading to features like muscle weakness, hypotonia, and areflexia.
  2. Symptoms:
    • Flaccid paralysis, especially in the lower limbs (as seen in the image).
    • Muscle wasting and deformities due to prolonged denervation.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Substantia gelatinosa nucleus: This is involved in sensory functions (pain and temperature modulation) and is not affected in poliomyelitis.

 

Option B. Dorsal horn cells: These cells relay sensory input and are also spared in poliomyelitis.

 

Option D. All of the above: This is incorrect, as only ventral horn cells are damaged.

 

Educational objective:

 

Poliomyelitis selectively damages ventral horn cells in the spinal cord, causing flaccid paralysis and motor deficits without affecting sensory functions. The correct answer is C.

questions.stem: Zenker’s diverticula is seen in between:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Cricopharyngeus & Thyropharyngeus

 

Zenker's diverticulum is an outpouching of the mucosal layer of the pharynx that occurs through a natural weak spot between the cricopharyngeus and thyropharyngeus muscles, which are parts of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor.

 

Key Features:

 

  1. Location:
    • The weak spot is called Killian's dehiscence, located between the fibers of the cricopharyngeus (horizontal fibers) and thyropharyngeus (oblique fibers).
    • This area is predisposed to herniation of the pharyngeal mucosa.
  2. Pathology:
    • Increased intraluminal pressure (e.g., due to swallowing dysfunction or cricopharyngeal muscle spasm) forces the mucosa through this weak area, forming a diverticulum.
  3. Clinical Features:
    • Dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested food, bad breath (halitosis), and potential aspiration.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Superior & Inferior constrictor: Incorrect, as Zenker's diverticulum occurs within the inferior constrictor, specifically between its parts.

 

Option C. Middle & Inferior constrictor: Incorrect, as the weak point is not located between these muscles.

 

Option D. Superior & Middle constrictor: Incorrect, as this region is not relevant to Zenker's diverticulum.

 

Educational objective:

 

Zenker’s diverticulum occurs in the weak area between the cricopharyngeus and thyropharyngeus muscles, which are components of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor.

Ans. B) Elongated styloid process

 

Eagle’s syndrome is a condition caused by an elongated styloid process or calcification of the stylohyoid ligament, leading to compression of nearby structures in the neck.

 

 

Key Features: 

 

  1. Anatomy:
    • The styloid process is a slender, pointed bone projecting from the temporal bone.
    • When elongated or calcified, it may compress adjacent structures, such as the internal carotid artery, external carotid artery, or cranial nerves (e.g., glossopharyngeal nerve).
  2. Clinical Presentation:
    • Pain: Throat pain, facial pain, or referred pain to the ear (glossopharyngeal neuralgia-like symptoms).
    • Dysphagia: Difficulty swallowing due to compression of the pharyngeal structures.
    • Vascular Symptoms: Dizziness or syncope due to compression of the carotid artery.
  3. Diagnosis:
    • Diagnosed via imaging (e.g., X-ray or CT scan) showing an elongated styloid process.
  4. Treatment:
    • Surgical removal of the elongated styloid process (styloidectomy) may alleviate symptoms.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Elongated mastoid process: Incorrect, as the mastoid process does not contribute to Eagle’s syndrome.

 

Option C. Short mastoid process: Irrelevant; no clinical condition is associated with a short mastoid process in this context.

 

Option D. Short styloid process: Incorrect; Eagle’s syndrome specifically involves an elongated styloid process.

 

Educational objective:

 

Eagle’s syndrome results from an elongated styloid process, which can compress nearby vascular and neural structures, leading to pain and dysphagia.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following indicated area is involved in pain relieving in case of massage at painful site:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) A

 

Nucleus of Substantis gelatinosa is located in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord. This nucleus is responsible for the modulation of the pain.

 

When massage or external stimulation is applied to a painful site, it activates mechanoreceptors that modulate the pain signals being transmitted by nociceptors (pain receptors). This phenomenon is part of the gate control theory of pain.

 

Key Features

:

  1. Substantia Gelatinosa (A):
    • Located in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord.
    • Involved in processing pain and temperature sensations.
    • Functions as a "gate" for pain modulation by inhibiting the transmission of nociceptive signals through mechanoreceptor activation.
  2. Massage or other external stimuli activates larger diameter mechanoreceptor fibers (A-beta fibers), which inhibit smaller diameter pain fibers (C fibers and A-delta fibers), thereby reducing the perception of pain.

 

Note:

 

  • The gray matter is divided into 10 lamina based on histocytochemistry.
  • Lamina 2 contains the substantia gelatinosa nucleus.
  • Substantia gelatinosa is involved in the pain and temperature pathway.
  • Lamina 2 is emphasized as the most important lamina due to its role in the pain and temperature pathway.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. B: Indicates an area adjacent to the dorsal horn but not directly responsible for pain modulation.

 

Option C. C: Corresponds to ventral regions, involved in motor control and unrelated to pain modulation.

 

Option D. D: The anterior column and ventral horn are primarily motor regions and do not contribute to pain modulation.

 

Educational objective:

 

The dorsal horn, particularly the substantia gelatinosa, is responsible for pain modulation during a massage at a painful site. This supports the gate control theory of pain, which explains the mechanism of pain relief through external stimulation. The correct answer is A.

questions.stemHtml: Congenital absence of shown muscle is known as?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Poland syndrome 

 

The image shows the pectoralis major muscle, a large, fan-shaped muscle of the chest involved in movements such as adduction, flexion, and medial rotation of the humerus. The congenital absence of the pectoralis major muscle is a characteristic feature of Poland syndrome.

 

Key Features of Poland Syndrome:

 

  1. Definition: A rare congenital condition characterized by the unilateral absence or underdevelopment of the pectoralis major muscle.
  2. Clinical Features:
    • Absence or hypoplasia of the pectoralis major, often on the right side.
    • Associated with abnormalities like underdeveloped chest wall and syndactyly (fusion of fingers) on the same side.
  3. Cause: Thought to result from a disruption in the embryonic blood supply, specifically to the subclavian artery.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Holland syndrome: There is no such syndrome named in clinical contexts.

 

Option C. Erb’s palsy: A brachial plexus injury involving the upper trunk (C5-C6 roots), causing weakness in shoulder and arm movements, not associated with muscle absence.

 

Option D. Klumpke’s syndrome: Another brachial plexus injury involving the lower trunk (C8-T1 roots), causing weakness in hand muscles and claw hand, unrelated to the pectoralis major.

 

Educational objective:

 

Poland syndrome is defined by the congenital absence or underdevelopment of the pectoralis major muscle and is often associated with ipsilateral hand anomalies. The correct answer is A. Poland syndrome.

questions.stemHtml: A sport person was doing weight lifting exercise. During exercise he got abnormal excessive stretching & visited the OPD with following symptom. Which nerve is damaged?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Nerve of Bell 

 

The clinical image shows winging of the scapula, a condition characterized by the elevation and protrusion of the medial border of the scapula. 

 

This clinical picture is obtained when there is weakness or paralysis of the serratus anterior muscle which is supplied by the long thoracic nerve also known as the nerve of bell.


Serratus anterior is known as the boxer's muscles as it is responsible for the forward protrusion (protraction) of the shoulder joint. In the case of palsy of this muscle when we ask the patient to press against the wall the medial border of the scapula tends to protrude backwards.

 

Key Features:

 

  1. Nerve of Bell (Long Thoracic Nerve):
    • Origin: C5, C6, C7 roots of the brachial plexus.
    • Function: Supplies the serratus anterior muscle, which anchors the scapula to the thoracic wall.
    • Damage: Results in weakness or paralysis of the serratus anterior, causing winging of the scapula.
  2. Causes:
    • Excessive stretching during weightlifting or trauma.
    • Iatrogenic injury during surgeries such as axillary lymph node dissection.
  3. Clinical Test:
    • Ask the patient to push against a wall. If the medial border of the scapula protrudes, it indicates paralysis of the serratus anterior.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Thoracodorsal nerve: Supplies the latissimus dorsi muscle, which is responsible for shoulder adduction and internal rotation, unrelated to scapular winging.

 

Option B. Subscapular nerve: Supplies the subscapularis muscle, involved in shoulder internal rotation, not scapular stabilization.

 

Option C. Nerve to subclavius: Supplies the subclavius muscle, involved in stabilizing the clavicle, unrelated to scapular winging.

 

Educational objective:

 

Winging of the scapula is caused by damage to the long thoracic nerve (Nerve of Bell), resulting in paralysis of the serratus anterior muscle. The correct answer is D. Nerve of Bell.

questions.stemHtml: Vessel present at the marked point:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Middle meningeal

 

The marked point corresponds to the pterion, a region on the lateral side of the skull where several cranial bones (frontal, parietal, temporal, and sphenoid) meet. The middle meningeal artery, a branch of the maxillary artery, runs deep to this area within the cranium.

 

Key Features:

 

Anatomy:

 

  • The middle meningeal artery enters the cranium through the foramen spinosum.
  • It supplies the dura mater and cranial bones.

Clinical Relevance:

  • The pterion is a thin and fragile area of the skull.
  • Trauma to this area can rupture the middle meningeal artery, leading to an epidural hematoma (extra-dural hemorrhage).
  • Symptoms include a "lucid interval" followed by rapid deterioration due to rising intracranial pressure.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Temporal: Refers to the superficial temporal artery, which is more superficial and not directly related to the marked point.

 

Option C. Carotid: The internal carotid artery runs deeper within the cranial cavity and is not associated with the pterion.

 

Option D. Maxillary: The maxillary artery is the parent artery of the middle meningeal artery but is not directly present at the marked point.

 

Educational objective:

 

The middle meningeal artery lies deep to the pterion, and trauma at this site can result in an epidural hematoma.

Ans. A) Card test

 

The Card Test is a clinical test used to assess the function of the ulnar nerve. The ulnar nerve innervates the palmar interossei muscles, which are responsible for finger adduction.

 

  • During the test, the patient is asked to hold a card between their fingers (typically the thumb and index finger). If the ulnar nerve is compromised, the patient will be unable to adduct the fingers effectively, leading to weakness or failure of the test.

 

Key Points:

 

  • The palmar interossei muscles are supplied by the ulnar nerve, and their function is tested in this maneuver.
  • A positive Card Test may indicate ulnar nerve dysfunction, such as in Cubital Tunnel Syndrome or Guyon's Canal Syndrome.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Tinel’s sign: This is used to detect irritated nerves, commonly the median nerve, by tapping over the nerve and observing for tingling sensations. It is not specific to the ulnar nerve.

 

Option C. Phalen’s sign: This test evaluates median nerve compression in the carpal tunnel and is not related to the ulnar nerve.

 

Option D. Pen test: There is no specific "Pen test" used for evaluating the ulnar nerve.

 

Note:

 

Mnemonic for Ulnar Nerve Tests:  B C D E F G H

 

B - Book test: The patient holds a book between the thumb and index finger. Weakness in this test indicates ulnar nerve dysfunction due to impaired adduction.

 

C - Card test: Involves holding a card between fingers. Inability to perform this action suggests weakness of the palmar interossei muscles supplied by the ulnar nerve.

 

D - Adductor pollicis test: Also called the Froment’s sign. Assesses weakness in the adductor pollicis muscle, which is supplied by the ulnar nerve.

 

E - Egawa’s test: Evaluates the interosseous muscles. The patient is asked to move their middle finger side-to-side while keeping it extended.

 

F - Froment’s sign: Tests the adductor pollicis. The patient is asked to hold a sheet of paper between the thumb and index finger. In ulnar nerve dysfunction, the thumb flexes at the IP joint to compensate, indicating a positive Froment’s sign.

 

G - Guyon’s canal syndrome: Also called Handlebar palsy. Compression of the ulnar nerve in Guyon’s canal presents with sensory loss and weakness in ulnar-innervated muscles.

 

H - Handlebar palsy: Another name for Guyon’s canal syndrome, often seen in cyclists due to prolonged pressure on the ulnar nerve.

 

Educational objective:

 

The Card Test is a specific clinical test for assessing the ulnar nerve by evaluating the function of the palmar interossei muscles, which are responsible for finger adduction.

questions.stem: Nerve not related to the lateral wall of cavernous sinus?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) V2

 

The cavernous sinus is a venous sinus located on either side of the sella turcica. Several cranial nerves are associated with its lateral wall, while others pass through its central portion.

 

It is the recent update that V2 is not related to the lateral wall of cavernous sinus, rather it is in the floor of caverous sinus.

 

The following nerves are embedded in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus:

 

 

  • Cranial Nerve III (Oculomotor nerve) 
  • Cranial Nerve IV (Trochlear nerve)
  • V1 (Ophthalmic division of Trigeminal nerve)
  • Nerves Passing Through the Cavernous Sinus (Not in the Wall):  Cranial Nerve VI (Abducens nerve) lies freely within the cavernous sinus, near the internal carotid artery.

 

Nerves Not in the Lateral Wall: V2 (Maxillary division of Trigeminal nerve) travels inferiorly and does not contribute to the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus. It passes through the foramen rotundum instead.

 

Educational objective:

 

The maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve (V2) is not related to the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus, as it exits the skull via the foramen rotundum.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the spinal segment?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Thoracic

 

The image shows a cross-section of a spinal cord segment with the following features, characteristic of the thoracic segment:

 

  1. Lateral Horn (Intermediate Horn):
    • The presence of a lateral horn is a hallmark of thoracic and upper lumbar segments (T1-L2), as it gives origin to sympathetic fibers of the autonomic nervous system.
    • Sympathetic outflow occurs exclusively from the thoracolumbar region.
  2. Dorsal and Ventral Horns:
    • The dorsal horn is associated with sensory nerve roots.
    • The ventral horn contains motor neurons but appears less prominent in the thoracic region compared to cervical or lumbar segments.
  3. Smaller Gray Matter:
    • The thoracic segment has relatively less gray matter compared to cervical or lumbar regions due to fewer motor neuron requirements for limb movement.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Cervical: The cervical region has larger gray matter due to the cervical enlargement for the brachial plexus and no lateral horn.

 

Option C. Lumbar: The lumbar region also has lateral horns but is characterized by a larger ventral horn for motor control of the lower limbs.

 

Option D. Sacral: The sacral region has significant gray matter for parasympathetic output and is part of the craniosacral outflow, not thoracolumbar.

 

Educational objective:

 

The thoracic spinal segment is identifiable by the presence of a lateral horn, which gives rise to sympathetic fibers, and smaller gray matter compared to cervical and lumbar regions. This segment is marked as B. Thoracic.

questions.stemHtml: Shown clinical situation occurs due to:

options.label: A
options.text: Fibrosis of Suspensory ligaments of cooper

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Fibrosis of lactiferous glands

 

The clinical image shows retraction of the nipple, a characteristic sign seen in breast carcinoma. Retraction occurs due to fibrosis and shrinkage of the lactiferous glands and ducts, caused by tumor infiltration.

 

Key Features:

 

  1. Mechanism of Nipple Retraction:
    • Fibrosis due to carcinoma involves the lactiferous glands and ducts.
    • This fibrosis causes the ducts to shrink and retract, pulling the nipple inward.
  2. Differentiation from Other Signs:
    • Peau d’orange appearance: Caused by obstruction of lymphatics leading to fibrosis of the suspensory ligaments of Cooper, resulting in dimpling of the skin.
    • Dimpling of the skin: Also due to fibrosis of suspensory ligaments, but it presents as skin puckering, not nipple retraction.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Fibrosis of Suspensory ligaments of Cooper: Involved in skin dimpling or peau d’orange, not nipple retraction.

 

Option C. Fibrosis of parenchyma of breast: While fibrosis can occur in breast parenchyma during cancer progression, it is not the primary cause of nipple retraction.

 

Option D. Fibrosis of lymphatics of breast: This leads to lymphatic obstruction and peau d’orange appearance, not nipple retraction.

 

Educational objective:

 

Nipple retraction in breast carcinoma occurs due to fibrosis of the lactiferous glands and ducts, causing them to shrink and pull the nipple inward. The correct answer is B. Fibrosis of lactiferous glands.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the cavity of the structure which acts as sensory gate way?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) B

 

The thalamus acts as the sensory gateway of the body, since all the afferents which are received from the body are related to thalamus and then from thalamus to cerebral cortex except for olfaction.Thalamus is the part of diencephalon. The cavity of diencephalon is called the third ventricle.

 

Key Features of the Thalamus and Its Cavity:

 

  1. Thalamus:
    • Functions as a relay station for sensory inputs like touch, pain, temperature, and vision to the cerebral cortex.
    • All sensations, except olfactory signals, pass through the thalamus. Recent research suggests some olfactory pathways might involve the thalamus indirectly.
  2. Third Ventricle:
    • The cavity of the diencephalon, where the thalamus is located.
    • It lies between the two halves of the thalamus and is marked as B in the image.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. A: Represents the lateral ventricle, which is the cavity of the cerebral hemispheres, unrelated to the thalamus.

 

Option C. C: Represents the cerebral aqueduct (Aqueduct of Sylvius), the cavity of the midbrain, connecting the third and fourth ventricles.

 

Option D. D: Represents the fourth ventricle, which is the cavity of the hindbrain, including the cerebellum and brainstem.

 

Educational objective:

 

The thalamus, the sensory gateway of the body, is part of the diencephalon, and its cavity is the third ventricle, labeled as B in the image

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Felon

 

The image shows Felon, a painful bacterial infection of the distal pulp space of the finger. This infection is typically localized to the fingertip, causing swelling, redness, and intense pain.

Option D. Infection of finger: A generic term; felon is a specific condition affecting the fingertip.

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Tinel’s sign

 

In the image the examiner is tapping over the region of the carpal tunnel in order to elicit the tingling and numbness sensation or pins and needles sensation. 

 

Such a test is known as tinel’s test. It is commonly used to assess median nerve compression in carpal tunnel syndrome.

 

Key Features of Tinel’s Sign:

 

  1. Procedure:
    • Tap over the median nerve at the wrist (carpal tunnel region).
    • A positive sign is when the patient experiences tingling or pain radiating along the distribution of the nerve (thumb, index, middle, and radial side of the ring finger).
  2. Indication:
    • Used to detect carpal tunnel syndrome or other neuropathies involving nerve compression or irritation.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Phalen’s test: Involves flexing the wrists and holding the position to compress the median nerve, causing symptoms. It is another test for carpal tunnel syndrome but not demonstrated in the image.

 

 

 

Option C. Card test: Assesses ulnar nerve function by evaluating the ability to hold a card between the fingers, unrelated to this test. the image shown. This test is performed in order to check for the ulnar nerve injury.

 

Option D. Froment’s sign: Evaluates ulnar nerve function by testing the adductor pollicis muscle while holding a piece of paper, unrelated to this  test shown in the image.

 

Educational objective:

 

Tinel’s sign is a diagnostic test for carpal tunnel syndrome, where tapping over the median nerve causes tingling or pain in the affected distribution.

The image demonstrates Phalen’s test, a diagnostic test for carpal tunnel syndrome. This test involves flexing the wrists to compress the median nerve within the carpal tunnel.

 

Key Features of Phalen’s Test:

 

  1. Procedure:
    • The patient flexes their wrists fully (pressing the backs of the hands together) and holds the position for 30-60 seconds.
    • A positive test results in tingling, numbness, or pain in the distribution of the median nerve (thumb, index finger, middle finger, and radial half of the ring finger).
  2. Indication:
    • Used to confirm carpal tunnel syndrome, caused by compression of the median nerve in the carpal tunnel.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Tinel’s sign: Involves tapping the median nerve at the wrist to elicit tingling, unrelated to wrist flexion.

 

Option C. Card test: Assesses ulnar nerve function by evaluating the ability to hold a card between the fingers.

 

 

Option D. Froment’s sign: Evaluates ulnar nerve function by testing the strength of the adductor pollicis muscle while holding a piece of paper, unrelated to this test.

 

 

Educational objective:

 

Phalen’s test is a clinical test for diagnosing carpal tunnel syndrome, performed by flexing the wrists to compress the median nerve.

Ans. A) Median nerve 

 

The test shown in the image assesses the median nerve by evaluating the function of the abductor pollicis brevis muscle, which is responsible for thumb abduction. This muscle is innervated by the median nerve.

 

Key Features of the Test:

 

  1. Procedure:
    • The patient is asked to abduct their thumb (move it away from the palm in a plane perpendicular to the fingers).
    • Weakness or inability to perform this movement indicates median nerve dysfunction.
  2. Clinical Relevance:
    • Median nerve injury is commonly associated with conditions such as carpal tunnel syndrome or trauma affecting the wrist or forearm.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Radial nerve: Involved in wrist and finger extension, not thumb abduction.

 

Option C. Ulnar nerve: Responsible for adduction and fine movements of the fingers, unrelated to thumb abduction.

 

Option D. Axillary nerve: Responsible for shoulder abduction, unrelated to hand or thumb function.

 

Educational objective:

 

The test in the image evaluates the median nerve, specifically testing the function of the abductor pollicis brevis muscle, which is responsible for thumb abduction

questions.stemHtml: If indicated nerve is damaged then which sign or test is positive:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Gower’s sign

 

The image indicates the inferior gluteal nerve with a root value of L5, S1, S2. This nerve innervates the gluteus maximus muscle, which plays a key role in extending the hip, particularly during activities such as standing up from a seated position, climbing stairs, or running. Damage to this nerve results in weakness of the gluteus maximus and manifests as a positive Gower’s sign.

 

Key Points:

 

  1. Function of Inferior Gluteal Nerve:
    • Supplies the gluteus maximus muscle, which is critical for hip extension and maintaining an erect posture.
    • Damage results in difficulty rising from a sitting position or climbing stairs, leading to compensatory movements.
  2. Gower’s Sign:
    • The patient uses their hands to push off their thighs or floor to rise to a standing position.
    • Commonly observed in inferior gluteal nerve injury or conditions such as Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Trendelenburg’s sign: Associated with the superior gluteal nerve, which innervates the gluteus medius and minimus. It is unrelated to the inferior gluteal nerve and does not involve the gluteus maximus.

 

Option C. Trendelenburg’s test: Assesses stability of the pelvis and is also linked to the superior gluteal nerve.

 

Option D. Waddling sign: Indicates generalized weakness of the pelvic girdle, not specific to the inferior gluteal nerve.

 

Educational objective:

 

Damage to the inferior gluteal nerve, which innervates the gluteus maximus, results in difficulty rising from a seated position and a positive Gower’s sign.
